**Why Tides Happen**

Tides are one of nature’s most fascinating and predictable phenomena, caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun on Earth’s oceans. The Moon, being much closer to our planet than the Sun, has the strongest influence, though both contribute to the rise and fall of sea levels. Imagine the Earth’s oceans as a stretchy, fluid blanket covering the planet. The Moon’s gravity tugs at this blanket, pulling the water toward it and creating a bulge on the side of the Earth facing the Moon. This is the high tide. At the same time, another high tide forms on the opposite side of the Earth due to the centrifugal force caused by our planet’s rotation. These two bulges mean that most coastal areas experience two high tides and two low tides each day.

The Sun also plays a role, though its effect is about half that of the Moon because it’s so far away. When the Sun and Moon align—during a full moon or new moon—their gravitational forces combine, leading to higher high tides and lower low tides, known as spring tides. Conversely, when they are at right angles relative to Earth, during the first and third quarters of the moon, their forces partially cancel each other out, resulting in neap tides, which are less extreme.

The shape of the coastline and the ocean floor can greatly influence how tides behave. In some places, like the Bay of Fundy in Canada, the geography funnels the water into a narrow space, causing tides to rise and fall dramatically—up to 16 meters in some areas. In other places, the tides are barely noticeable. The Earth’s rotation, the Moon’s orbit around Earth, and the Sun’s position all work together to create these variations.
